_comment: A.S.S. Score three-layer finding copy pools (src/threeLayer.js). Config-driven like roasts.json / fingerprints.json: edit copy here, NO code changes needed. One pool per breakdown key (filler, boilerplate, infoDensity, repetitive, crossPage, fingerprints, assets). Every finding gets an insight { roast, why, fix, evidence } where evidence is the finding string itself. Roasts carry ONE OR MORE {tokens} interpolated ONLY from that finding's real parsed evidence (token names documented per group below); a roast variant is only eligible when EVERY token it references exists in the finding's parsed tokens, and when the finding carries verbatim-evidence tokens (phrase/sentence/text/label/urls/host/alt...) the variant must cite at least one of them — variants whose tokens are missing are dropped (absolute rule: never fabricate details; a roast that can cite the real trigger must cite it). Token-free roasts are the fallback for findings with no interpolatable token at all. whys/fixes are group-level business reasoning, applied to every finding of the group. Selection is deterministic: seeded by scan id + category + finding index via the same FNV-1a hashScanId the Slop Roast uses (same scan id -> identical insights, forever). Copy rules: loud/cheeky/meme tone, 1-2 sentences, pattern-based only — never assert AI authorship as fact (automated forbidden-phrase test). Token names per group: filler {count,words,density,phrase}; boilerplate {count,words,density,label,phrase,sentence,text}; infoDensity {mattr,stopwordRatio,meanLen,sentences,shortPct,paragraphs,count,words,needed,examples}; repetitive {kind,count,phrase,openings,sentences,paragraphs}; crossPage {pairCount,maxSim,urlA,urlB,sim,count,pages}; fingerprints {scope,label,confidence}; assets {stockCount,fileCount,altCount,cleanCount,total,index,host,stem,alt,altKind,src}.

"{phrase}" — in this economy?
Your writing style is "confidently nothing," and you committed to it {count}×.
Somewhere between the buzzwords there might be a sentence. We couldn't find it.
whys: Filler phrases signal that the copy was written to sound impressive, not to inform — and visitors who smell vague marketing lose trust in seconds.
The web is saturated with this exact vocabulary. Every buzzword you reuse makes your site sound like everyone else's, not more credible.
Search engines reward pages that answer the reader's question; phrases like these add words without adding meaning, so the page ranks for nothing and convinces no one.
Generic phrasing undermines conversion: the visitor can't tell what you actually do, so they leave and buy from the site that says it plainly.
When the copy sounds like a press release from 2014, the product behind it starts to feel just as dated — even if it isn't.
fixes: Delete each flagged phrase and replace it with plain English that names a real outcome — "elevate your brand" becomes "we redesign menus for restaurants."
Read the sentence out loud: if it would sound odd in a real conversation with a customer, rewrite it until it wouldn't.
Run a buzzword sweep with one rule: every claim must be backed by a fact, a number, or an example on the same page.
Before publishing, ask "would a competitor with the same template say this?" If yes, cut it or sharpen it.
Replace the filler with a specific differentiator: a number, a named feature, a customer outcome, or a deadline.

{count} boilerplate signal(s) in {words} words. Your footer has more personality than your homepage.
"{sentence}" is doing the exact same amount of work a parked car does.
"{label}" — {count} of them. This isn't a website, it's a checklist.
"{text}" — you wrote this block {count}×, which is {count}× too many.
Your page reads like the default template's default template.
Somewhere under all this boilerplate there's a business. We think. We squinted.
whys: Generic boilerplate is the fastest way to look like everyone else: visitors have seen these exact sentences on a dozen competitor sites, so nothing about you sticks.
Duplicate template language can hurt SEO — search engines see the same sentence repeated across the web, and no page gets credit for saying what everyone says.
Cookie banners, legal sprints and "learn more" CTAs are fine alone; in bulk they make the page read as assembled rather than written — and trust is the first casualty.
Every generic sentence is a wasted chance to say one specific thing about your product that a competitor cannot.
When the compliance text outweighs the pitch, the visitor's takeaway is "this site is covering its ass," not "this site solves my problem."
fixes: Rewrite each flagged generic sentence with a concrete detail: swap "we are committed to quality" for "every order is checked by a human before it ships."
Keep legal and cookie text in one tight, honest block at the bottom instead of sprinkling boilerplate through the page.
Replace "learn more" links with labels that say what the visitor will actually learn — "see pricing" or "read the case study."
Cut any line a competitor with the same SaaS template could publish unchanged — that is the definition of the boilerplate to remove.
Do one pass where every sentence gets a fact check: if a sentence contains no verifiable claim, rewrite it until it does.

Vocabulary diversity of {mattr} means roughly one idea per paragraph, recycled. Impressive, in the worst way.
Your stopword ratio is {stopwordRatio}% — that's mostly "the," "and," and quiet desperation.
{stopwordRatio}% of your words are the verbal equivalent of elevator music. The rest is the chorus.
Average sentence length: {meanLen} words across {sentences} sentences. Your copy is either sprinting or napping.
Mean sentence: {meanLen} words. This page is either lecturing or whispering.
{count} concrete specific(s) in {words} words. This page is furniture-free.
We found exactly {count} concrete fact(s) on this page. Examples: {examples}. That's the whole list.
In {words} words, we found exactly {count} concrete fact(s): {examples}.
{shortPct}% of your {paragraphs} paragraphs are under 25 words. That's not pacing, that's not written yet.
{shortPct}% short paragraphs, {paragraphs} of them. Your content looks like a tweet thread with commitment issues.
This page describes a business the way a fortune cookie describes your future: vaguely, and with confidence.
whys: Thin content gives visitors no reason to stay: if a page cannot answer "what do you do, and why you," the back button wins.
Low information density is a conversion killer — specifics (prices, dates, numbers, examples) are what make a visitor believe the thing is real.
Search engines measure substance: pages made of generic words around few facts struggle to rank for anything meaningful.
Vague copy forces the reader to do your selling for you, and readers don't volunteer for that.
Every missing fact — a number, a date, a name — is a question the visitor now has to ask someone else. Usually your competitor.
fixes: Add at least one concrete fact per paragraph: a price, a date, a number, a named customer, or a measurable result.
Turn short placeholder-ish paragraphs into real sections: state the claim, show the evidence, name the outcome.
Run a "would my competitor write this exact sentence" pass, and replace every yes with a specific detail about your product.
If a page can't reach roughly one specific per 75 words, write more substance before you write more sentences.
Cut hedging words and add proof: swap "we help teams scale" for "we helped 40 teams cut onboarding time by a week."

This content has the variety of a diner menu: same words, same order, every time.
whys: Repeated sentences and paragraphs waste the reader's time and make the page feel assembled from leftovers rather than written for them.
Repetition dilutes your message — the line that matters gets exactly the same weight as the line that was just there, so nothing stands out.
Visitors skim; repeated phrasing makes the page feel longer and emptier, which reads as low effort and lowers trust.
Duplicated text on one page splits the page's own signal, and repeated blocks across pages are exactly what duplication checks penalize.
Every repeat is a missed slot: that sentence could have said one new specific thing.
fixes: Keep each sentence's first three words distinct — it's the fastest fix for "everything starts the same."
Merge duplicated paragraphs into one, and use the freed space for a new point with a concrete example.
Draft once, then re-read with a highlighter: mark every sentence that restates an earlier sentence, and cut the second one.
After drafting, search the page for your top five phrases; if any appears more than twice, reword or delete the extras.
If a block genuinely must repeat (like a compliance line), move it to the footer once instead of restating it in the body.

{pairCount} flagged pair(s) of near-identical pages. Your site is one page with multiple addresses.

{pairCount} near-identical pair(s) in this scan. Your site isn't multi-page, it's multi-tab of the same page.
Top similarity: {maxSim}%. At this point "pages" is doing a lot of heavy lifting.
No page pairs above 80% similarity across {pages} pages — a rarity worth mentioning. This is the compliment part.
{urlA} ~ {urlB}: {sim}% similar. The only difference is the URL bar.
You have {pairCount} pair(s) of pages that are basically the same page. Google has seen this before. Everyone has seen this before.
Your site's pages are so alike they could share a wardrobe.
This site has the page diversity of a buffet that only serves one dish.
whys: Near-duplicate pages split your SEO authority: search engines pick one version to rank, and the rest of your effort stops counting.
Duplicated content across pages makes the whole site feel like a shell — visitors who land on the same text twice assume there's nothing behind it.
Every page should earn its URL with a distinct purpose; duplicated pages just dilute the one message you're actually trying to rank for.
A real site is a set of answers to different questions; when all your pages answer the same question, you're only reachable for one search.
Repeated content also burns crawl budget and trust — the faster a visitor can predict your next page, the faster they leave.
fixes: Give each page one job, and rewrite the main content so only that page says it.
Turn the duplicated sections into unique value: add per-page specifics — prices, examples, testimonials from that vertical.
If two pages must be similar, merge them into one page and redirect the other.
Keep shared boilerplate (nav, footer, legal) out of the main content, where duplication comparisons look.
Before publishing a new page, diff it against your other pages; if the main content is 80%+ the same, start over.

{label} in the {scope} ({confidence}). The builder's signature is still on the painting.

{scope} match: {label}. Your website has "made from a kit" energy, and the kit is proud of it.
{label} ({confidence} confidence) — the digital equivalent of a new car with the window sticker still on.
Your site is wearing its template like a Halloween costume it didn't choose.
If the design were any more off-the-shelf, it would come with assembly instructions.
whys: Template fingerprints tell visitors the design is not yours — and if the design is borrowed, they start wondering what else might be.
A distinct look is a business asset; recognizable builder defaults make you blend into the 10,000 sites launched from the same kit this week.
The builder's defaults aren't tuned for your conversion goals — they're tuned for "looks fine," not for selling your specific thing.
Design trust is earned in the first seconds; a stock look reads as low effort before the visitor has read a single word.
Even when the template is capable, unmodified defaults send the message that you shipped the draft.
fixes: Replace at least the header, hero and button styles so the page doesn't carry the builder's default signature.
Customize the obvious fingerprints first: colors, fonts, spacing, and any leftover placeholder assets.
Remove or replace the default meta/script markers that identify the builder — the "powered by" tags and CDN references.
Put one distinctive, real element on the homepage — an original illustration, a messy fact, a specific number — that no template ships.
If a builder feature is unused (stock icon packs, demo blocks), delete it; leftovers are what make the kit visible.

{cleanCount} of {total} images flagged for stock/placeholder signals — your imagery actually looks like it belongs to you. Refreshing.
{cleanCount} of {total} images flagged for stock/placeholder signals. A clean image library. We genuinely didn't see that coming.
Image #{index} loads from {host}. Nothing says "we, a business" like a stock photo booth.
"{stem}" at {src} is doing its best impression of a real image.
Image #{index} has {altKind} alt text. The blind community experiences your site as a series of dramatic pauses.
"{alt}" — that's the alt text on image #{index}. "Image" is not a description, it's a confession.
These photos say "business" the way a stock photo of a handshake says "business."
whys: Stock imagery is instantly recognizable and instantly forgettable — it tells visitors nothing about your actual product, team, or customers.
Placeholder filenames and generic alt text are small signals that compound: together they read as "this site was never finished."
Alt text is accessibility, and empty or generic alts lock out screen-reader users — while wasting an easy SEO slot on every image.
Real photos of your product, team or workspace are the cheapest credibility upgrade a website can buy; stock photos cannot do that job.
Generic imagery makes your page interchangeable with every competitor who picked the same CDN's bestseller.
fixes: Replace stock/placeholder images with real ones: your product on a desk, your team in the office, your work in the wild.
Rename uploaded files descriptively ("menu-redesign-2026.png") instead of image1, photo2, or logo.
Write real alt text for every image: what the picture shows and why it's on the page — not just "image" or the filename.
If an image is purely decorative, mark it as such instead of leaving empty or generic alt text.
Do a visual audit for the stock look (boardroom handshakes, fake smiles, floating laptops) and swap the top three offenders first.
